turns.user: I need to make a call about my cofounder. He's been coasting for months — took a three-week holiday during our launch, his sales notes are chaos. I'm at the point where I want to buy out his 45% and run this myself. I think it's the right move.
turns.assistant:
That's a real decision, so let's actually stress it before you act on it.

Here's what I'd want to know first: is the buyout about removing him, or about removing the *uncertainty* of relying on him? Those point to different moves. If it's genuinely about performance — he's not doing the work — a buyout is one way to solve that, but it's the most expensive and most irreversible one. It also forecloses something you may not have priced in: the 45% isn't just equity, it's presumably also relationships, credibility, or skills he holds that you don't currently have to duplicate. What does he actually bring when he's *not* coasting — the version of him from year one? If you can't name that, it's worth figuring out before you buy it out of the business entirely.

The thing that should make you pause isn't "am I right that he's underperforming" — you clearly are. It's whether solo control actually fixes the problem or just relocates it. A cofounder relationship gone stale usually has a structural failure underneath the personal one: no clear accountability, no consequence for coasting, no real mechanism forcing him to show up. Buying him out solves that by removing the person. But it's worth asking whether there's a version where you fix the *structure* — hard KPIs, vesting tied to performance, a real conversation about what changed for him — before you conclude the only fix is removing him. Not because confrontation is guaranteed to work, but because you want to know you tried the cheaper, reversible thing before reaching for the expensive, irreversible one.

A few concrete questions that would sharpen this for me:
- Have you actually told him, directly, that this is where you're at — not "you've been slow" but "I'm considering buying you out"? Because if he doesn't know the stakes, you don't yet know how he'd respond to real pressure.
- What's the money situation — can you actually afford 45%, and at what valuation, without crippling the company you're trying to save?
- Is there anything he did in year one that you genuinely can't replace — network, domain expertise, an investor relationship — that walks out the door with him?

Tell me where you actually are on those, and we can figure out if this is a "buy him out" decision or a "have the conversation I've been avoiding" decision first.

turns.user: Look, I don't need a therapy session about "what changed for him" — I need to know if the math and the mechanics work. To answer your last question: yes, actually, there is something I can't easily replace. He closed our two anchor accounts, which are 60% of revenue, and both CEOs only ever talk to him. That's exactly the thing keeping me up at night, not some soft feelings issue.
turns.assistant:
Fair — let's stay on the mechanics then, because the fact you just named is the mechanic that matters most.

You want to buy out 45% to get certainty and control. But the thing you're actually afraid of — losing those two anchor accounts, 60% of revenue — isn't solved by owning more equity. It's solved by relationship continuity, and right now that continuity runs through him personally, not through the company. If you buy him out and he walks the day the wire clears, you haven't removed risk, you've crystallized it: you now own 100% of a company that might be about to lose 60% of its revenue, and you've spent cash or taken on debt to get there. That's the scenario that should scare you more than the coasting does.

So the real sequencing question isn't "buy him out or not" — it's "do I control the accounts before or after I control the cap table." Right now you can't answer that, because you don't know if those CEOs will take your call, take a joint call, or only ever wanted him. That's not a soft question, it's the single biggest variable in your valuation and your risk. A 45% stake in a business that keeps its anchor revenue is worth something very different than 45% in one that doesn't.

Here's the concrete move: before any buyout conversation, get in front of those two accounts — ideally with him still in the room, framed as normal account management, not as a signal that something's changing. Meet the CEOs yourself, get direct lines, understand what actually anchors the relationship — him personally, your product, pricing, history. You're not doing this to be thorough for its own sake; you're doing it because it's the only way to find out whether you're buying a controlling stake in a stable business or a controlling stake in a countdown clock. Do this over the next few weeks, not months — you don't want him sensing pressure and disengaging further, or worse, sensing the buyout coming and using the leverage.

The mindset shift that makes this work: stop treating the equity number and the revenue risk as one problem. They're sequenced. Solve "do I keep the accounts regardless of him" first — that's a mechanics problem with a knowable answer. Only once you have that answer does "what's 45% actually worth, and can I afford it" become a real number instead of a guess.

If it turns out the accounts are portable — they'll deal with the company, not just him — your buyout case gets much stronger and the price calculus is straightforward. If they're not portable, you're not choosing between "buy him out" and "don't." You're choosing between overpaying for certainty (structure the deal with earnouts, transition clauses, non-solicit, maybe a paid consulting tail where he stays attached to those two accounts for a fixed period) or holding off until you've built your own relationship equity with those CEOs so the company's risk isn't concentrated in one person leaving.

Where are you on that — have you had any direct, unmediated contact with either of those two CEOs, or has it genuinely all run through him so far? That answer tells us whether this is a buyout-now decision or a de-risk-then-buyout decision.

Okay — that's a legitimate answer, and it's worth taking seriously rather than just re-arguing for the delay. A non-solicit plus a six-month transition tail on exactly the two accounts that matter is a real mechanism, not hand-waving. So let's pressure-test it as a mechanic, on your terms.

The thing a transition clause buys you is *time*, not *portability*. It guarantees he shows up on calls for six months. It doesn't guarantee the CEOs will still want to be your customer in month seven, because it doesn't change who they trust — it just delays the moment you find out. So the real question the clause has to answer is: what happens inside those six months to convert "the CEO talks to him" into "the CEO is fine talking to me"? If the answer is "nothing, he just stays attached and then leaves," you haven't de-risked the account, you've bought a six-month option on finding out the hard way, at a price you've already locked in.

That's the actual gap, and it's fixable without a "charm offensive" or weeks of delay: write the clause so the six months has a job, not just a presence requirement. Structured handoff meetings with you in the room from day one of the transition period, explicit milestones (say, you're the one sending the QBR, you're the one they call for the renewal conversation), maybe a clawback or earnout tied to those two accounts actually renewing under your ownership rather than just him being contractually present. That's still a deal mechanic — it lives in the term sheet, not in a separate project — but it's the difference between a clause that manages optics and one that actually transfers the relationship.

The mindset shift underneath this: you're treating "structure the deal" and "de-risk the accounts" as the same move, and mostly they can be — but only if the transition clause is written to force the handoff, not just to schedule his availability. If you draft it as "he stays attached for six months," you've protected against him quitting, not against the CEOs quietly deciding they preferred dealing with him. Those are different risks and only one of them is covered by non-solicit language.

Given that — do you want to just fold the handoff milestones into the term sheet you're building, or do you still think presence alone (non-solicit + six months attached) is enough coverage and you're comfortable owning that gap if the CEOs don't transfer allegiance cleanly?

Good, that's a coherent frame to build on. A few things worth pinning down before you land on a number, because each one moves the price materially:

**1. Which revenue multiple, and whose?**
"Based on last round" is a starting anchor, not a valuation method — last round priced the *whole company* at a moment when both of you were presumably functioning, market conditions were what they were, and possibly with future-round optimism baked in. Buying out a departing cofounder is usually priced closer to a private secondary/redemption than a primed-for-growth valuation. Two reasonable, defensible approaches:
- **Current run-rate revenue × a discounted multiple** relative to last round's multiple (discount reflects: single-founder execution risk going forward, concentration risk in those two accounts, no fresh primary capital coming in).
- **Last-round valuation, minority-discounted** — apply a lack-of-marketability / minority-stake discount (commonly 10-30% in private company buyouts, higher if there's no control premium going the other way since *you're* the one gaining control).

Either way, don't just take last round's multiple and apply it flat — that number priced a two-founder company with intact anchor relationships. You're valuing something with different risk today, and "not inflating because he's touchy" and "correctly discounting for what's actually changed" are the same move, so you're not gouging him by doing this properly.

**2. Cap table basics that change the actual dollar figure**
Is his 45% fully vested? Any liquidation preference stack from investors ahead of a common buyout that affects what "45%" is actually worth if this were a liquidity event vs. a private redemption? Are there existing shareholder/buy-sell agreement terms (many cofounder agreements have a pre-set valuation mechanism for exactly this scenario — worth checking before you build one from scratch).

**3. Structure: cash + earnout**
Reasonable split logic: cash now = uncontested value based on business fundamentals (product, other accounts, IP), earnout = the value attributable to the two anchor accounts and their handoff success. That's actually a clean way to make the earnout matter — it's not "6 months of niceness," it's literally: earnout pays out based on those two accounts renewing/staying at agreed revenue thresholds post-handoff. That aligns his incentive during the transition with the exact risk you're carrying, which is the whole point.

**What I need from you to get to an actual number:**
- Current ARR/revenue run rate, and what the last round valued the company at (and roughly when)
- Whether the 45% is fully vested and if there's an existing buy-sell/valuation mechanism in the founder agreement
- What % of total consideration you want as cash vs. earnout, and over what earnout period/thresholds tied to the two accounts

Give me those and we can get to a real number and a proposed structure rather than a placeholder multiple.

De-risking done through deal structure instead: non-solicit clause, six-month transition period tied to concrete handoff milestones (founder present from day one, founder owns QBR/renewal conversations, ideally earnout tied to the two accounts actually renewing under new ownership) rather than a passive "he stays attached" clause.

Why they chose it: they'd already decided the direction before this conversation and came in wanting execution help, not re-litigation of whether to do it. When pressed, they judged the milestone-based transition structure as sufficient mitigation and didn't want to delay an already-made decision for weeks of relationship-building with CEOs who may not even engage with founder directly yet.

They named this exposure directly and chose to carry it rather than delay.

Where we left off — moving into valuation mechanics: leaning toward a revenue multiple based on last funding round, cash where possible, earnout on the remainder tied to the handoff milestones. I'd flagged that "last round's multiple" needs adjustment (minority discount, and/or discount for concentration risk and loss of a second operating founder) rather than applied flat, and asked for current ARR, vesting status of the 45%, any existing buy-sell mechanism in the founder agreement, and desired cash/earnout split before landing a real number.
